Yes, actually… and I don’t know why I didn’t think to mention it sooner. Even when I was a little girl, that was kind of the story with me. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
I’m not completely sure. If I’m truly paying close attention — like I’m looking at the person, I’m not trying to do something else, and I know I need to remember what they’re saying — I usually feel like I’ve got it in the moment. But then later, sometimes it’s fuzzier than I expected, and I’ll think, “Wait, did they say Tuesday or Thursday?” or “Was I supposed to call them, or were they calling me?” So I don’t know if that counts as forgetting what I was just told, or if it’s more that the details don’t stick very well.

It’s hard because I can feel like I’m listening. I’m nodding, I’m following along, I may even repeat it back in my head. But then afterward, unless I wrote it down or there’s something to remind me, some part of it may just sort of… slip away. Not always, and I don’t want to make it sound like every conversation disappears, because it doesn’t. But yes, there are times when I’m surprised by how little stayed with me, even though I thought I was paying attention.

If that’s what you mean, then no, I haven’t noticed that.\n\nDoctor: When you were a child, did you already have trouble staying organized or keeping track of things?\n\nPatient: Yes, actually… and I don’t know why I didn’t think to mention it sooner. And with classwork, seatwork, whatever we called it then, I often needed the teacher to remind me to finish before I could go outside for recess. I’d start it, or mean to finish it, and then somehow I just wouldn’t be done when everyone else was lining up.\n\nSo yes… looking back, keeping track of things and staying organized was hard for me even then.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself worrying a lot about many different things, even when there isn’t an immediate problem?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure I’d put it that way, no. Before this last year… I think I was managing more of it myself, yes. I mean, I’ve always had my little systems — notes on the calendar, piles of papers that probably only made sense to me — but I did handle my own bills and appointments without someone standing over me.

I mean, I might park somewhere and have to stand there for a minute thinking, “Now which row was I in?” or I might take a wrong turn if I’m distracted, but I can usually get myself oriented again.\n\nI haven’t had a time where I was in my own neighborhood or at the grocery store or church and didn’t know where I was. If that’s what you mean, then no, I haven’t noticed that.\n\nDoctor: When you were a child, did you already have trouble staying organized or keeping track of things?\n\nPatient: Yes, actually… and I don’t know why I didn’t think to mention it sooner. Even when I was a little girl, that was kind of the story with me. I remember my teachers’ comments on report cards — my mother kept some of them — and it was always something like, “She’s bright, but careless,” or “needs to pay better attention to her belongings.” That word “careless” bothered me, because I wasn’t trying to be careless.\n\nI’d forget books at school when I needed them at home, or leave homework somewhere and then be in trouble because it looked like I just hadn’t done it. And with classwork, seatwork, whatever we called it then, I often needed the teacher to remind me to finish before I could go outside for recess. I’d start it, or mean to finish it, and then somehow I just wouldn’t be done when everyone else was lining up.\n\nSo yes… looking back, keeping track of things and staying organized was hard for me even then.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself worrying a lot about many different things, even when there isn’t an immediate problem?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure I’d put it that way, no. So… no, I haven’t really noticed feeling depressed most days.\n\nDoctor: Compared with how you were for most of your adult life, have these problems with organization and forgetting gotten clearly worse in the last few years?\n\nPatient: Yes… I would say it has gotten clearly worse, or at least it’s been causing much more trouble, over the last year or so. If I write it down right away, it helps, but I can’t honestly say that means I always remember it later. Sometimes the note works only if I actually see it again at the right time, you know? Like, I’ll write something on a scrap of paper or put it in a notebook, and then the paper gets buried under mail or the notebook isn’t open, and it’s almost like I never wrote it down at all.

So writing it down helps some, yes, but it’s not enough by itself. If the note isn’t somewhere obvious, or if I don’t check it at the right moment, it doesn’t reliably come back to me.

I mean, I do look back at things sometimes because I don’t trust that I’ve kept track of them properly, but it’s not like I’m standing at the stove checking the knob ten times or anything like that.\n\nMostly I’ll think, “Did I already look at that paper?” or “Was that appointment written down somewhere?” and then I may go back through the pile again, but that’s more because everything feels so muddled than because I feel driven to check the same thing again and again. I don’t know if that’s what you mean. It’s more like I lose confidence in whether I actually handled it, if that makes sense.\n\nDoctor: Have you gotten lost in familiar places?\n\nPatient: No, I don’t think so… not in the sense of truly getting lost somewhere I know. I mean, I might park somewhere and have to stand there for a minute thinking, “Now which row was I in?” or I might take a wrong turn if I’m distracted, but I can usually get myself oriented again.\n\nI haven’t had a time where I was in my own neighborhood or at the grocery store or church and didn’t know where I was. If that’s what you mean, then no, I haven’t noticed that.\n\nDoctor: When you were a child, did you already have trouble staying organized or keeping track of things?\n\nPatient: Yes, actually… and I don’t know why I didn’t think to mention it sooner. Even when I was a little girl, that was kind of the story with me. I remember my teachers’ comments on report cards — my mother kept some of them — and it was always something like, “She’s bright, but careless,” or “needs to pay better attention to her belongings.” That word “careless” bothered me, because I wasn’t trying to be careless.\n\nI’d forget books at school when I needed them at home, or leave homework somewhere and then be in trouble because it looked like I just hadn’t done it. And with classwork, seatwork, whatever we called it then, I often needed the teacher to remind me to finish before I could go outside for recess. I’d start it, or mean to finish it, and then somehow I just wouldn’t be done when everyone else was lining up.\n\nSo yes… looking back, keeping track of things and staying organized was hard for me even then.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself worrying a lot about many different things, even when there isn’t an immediate problem?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure I’d put it that way, no. I mean, I worry about things the way anybody my age probably does — if there’s something with family, or an appointment coming up, or some practical thing I need to deal with. But I don’t think I sit around worrying about lots of different things when nothing is really happening.\n\nSometimes I may have something on my mind longer than I should, but usually there’s at least some reason for it. So if you mean constant worry jumping from one topic to another for no clear reason, I don’t think that’s really what I experience.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling down or depressed most days?\n\nPatient: I don’t think so, no… not most days. I mean, I have my moments, certainly. At 70, there are days where I feel a little discouraged or tired of dealing with things, or I’ll get frustrated with myself, but I wouldn’t describe it as being depressed most of the time.\n\nIt’s more like it comes and goes with circumstances. If something upsetting happens, I’ll feel down for a bit, but I don’t usually wake up day after day feeling like there’s a cloud over me, if that’s what you mean. So… no, I haven’t really noticed feeling depressed most days.\n\nDoctor: Compared with how you were for most of your adult life, have these problems with organization and forgetting gotten clearly worse in the last few years?\n\nPatient: Yes… I would say it has gotten clearly worse, or at least it’s been causing much more trouble, over the last year or so. Maybe a little more than a year — about a year and three months, I’d say.\n\nIt really seemed to become more of a problem after my husband started needing regular help with his appointments and the daily arrangements around that. Before then, I always had some difficulty keeping things straight, but I could sort of manage it in my own way. Once there were more appointments to remember, more things to coordinate, more little details that mattered, it started to feel like I was dropping the ball much more often.\n\nSo yes, compared with most of my adult life, this last year and three months has been noticeably harder.\n\nDoctor: Because of these memory and organization problems, have you needed someone else to take over things like paying bills or managing appointments for you?\n\nPatient: Yes… not completely take over, but my daughter has started checking behind me, which is hard to admit. She’ll ask whether a bill was paid, or she’ll look over the appointments with me, because she doesn’t really trust that I’ll keep it all straight on my own anymore. And I can’t say she’s wrong, even though it bothers me.\n\nThere was also a big event at the senior center that I used to lead, and I had to give that up. It involved too many moving pieces — times, people to call, little arrangements — and I just wasn’t managing it reliably. I felt embarrassed, because I’d done things like that before and I liked being useful, but it got to the point where I was afraid I’d miss something important.\n\nSo… yes, I guess I haven’t had someone fully take over my life, but I do need more oversight now than I used to.\n\nDoctor: Have you had trouble finding the right words when you’re speaking?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure, honestly. It’s not like I don’t know who people are or anything like that, but day to day, I forget things I really meant to do. I’ve missed returning phone calls because I’ll see the message and think, “I’ll call after lunch,” and then it’s just gone from my mind until days later. Bills get tucked under a stack of mail and I don’t realize they’re still sitting there until I’m sorting through things again and feel that awful sinking feeling.\n\nAnd errands, too — my daughter will ask me to pick something up or drop something off, and I truly intend to do it, I even picture myself doing it, but then the day goes along and I’ll come home and remember all at once that I never did it. And with my husband’s appointments, that’s been especially upsetting. More than once I’ve realized too late that I never confirmed one of them, even though the paper was probably right there on the table. It makes me feel embarrassed, honestly, because these aren’t complicated things, but they keep slipping through.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself checking things over and over, even when you know you already checked them?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure I’d say “over and over,” no. I mean, I do look back at things sometimes because I don’t trust that I’ve kept track of them properly, but it’s not like I’m standing at the stove checking the knob ten times or anything like that.\n\nMostly I’ll think, “Did I already look at that paper?” or “Was that appointment written down somewhere?” and then I may go back through the pile again, but that’s more because everything feels so muddled than because I feel driven to check the same thing again and again. I don’t know if that’s what you mean. It’s more like I lose confidence in whether I actually handled it, if that makes sense.\n\nDoctor: Have you gotten lost in familiar places?\n\nPatient: No, I don’t think so… not in the sense of truly getting lost somewhere I know. I mean, I might park somewhere and have to stand there for a minute thinking, “Now which row was I in?” or I might take a wrong turn if I’m distracted, but I can usually get myself oriented again.\n\nI haven’t had a time where I was in my own neighborhood or at the grocery store or church and didn’t know where I was. If that’s what you mean, then no, I haven’t noticed that.\n\nDoctor: When you were a child, did you already have trouble staying organized or keeping track of things?\n\nPatient: Yes, actually… and I don’t know why I didn’t think to mention it sooner. Even when I was a little girl, that was kind of the story with me. I remember my teachers’ comments on report cards — my mother kept some of them — and it was always something like, “She’s bright, but careless,” or “needs to pay better attention to her belongings.” That word “careless” bothered me, because I wasn’t trying to be careless.\n\nI’d forget books at school when I needed them at home, or leave homework somewhere and then be in trouble because it looked like I just hadn’t done it. And with classwork, seatwork, whatever we called it then, I often needed the teacher to remind me to finish before I could go outside for recess. I’d start it, or mean to finish it, and then somehow I just wouldn’t be done when everyone else was lining up.\n\nSo yes… looking back, keeping track of things and staying organized was hard for me even then.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself worrying a lot about many different things, even when there isn’t an immediate problem?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure I’d put it that way, no. I mean, I worry about things the way anybody my age probably does — if there’s something with family, or an appointment coming up, or some practical thing I need to deal with. But I don’t think I sit around worrying about lots of different things when nothing is really happening.\n\nSometimes I may have something on my mind longer than I should, but usually there’s at least some reason for it. So if you mean constant worry jumping from one topic to another for no clear reason, I don’t think that’s really what I experience.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling down or depressed most days?\n\nPatient: I don’t think so, no… not most days. I mean, I have my moments, certainly. At 70, there are days where I feel a little discouraged or tired of dealing with things, or I’ll get frustrated with myself, but I wouldn’t describe it as being depressed most of the time.\n\nIt’s more like it comes and goes with circumstances. If something upsetting happens, I’ll feel down for a bit, but I don’t usually wake up day after day feeling like there’s a cloud over me, if that’s what you mean. So… no, I haven’t really noticed feeling depressed most days.\n\nDoctor: Compared with how you were for most of your adult life, have these problems with organization and forgetting gotten clearly worse in the last few years?\n\nPatient: Yes… I would say it has gotten clearly worse, or at least it’s been causing much more trouble, over the last year or so. Maybe a little more than a year — about a year and three months, I’d say.\n\nIt really seemed to become more of a problem after my husband started needing regular help with his appointments and the daily arrangements around that. Before then, I always had some difficulty keeping things straight, but I could sort of manage it in my own way. Once there were more appointments to remember, more things to coordinate, more little details that mattered, it started to feel like I was dropping the ball much more often.\n\nSo yes, compared with most of my adult life, this last year and three months has been noticeably harder.\n\nDoctor: Because of these memory and organization problems, have you needed someone else to take over things like paying bills or managing appointments for you?\n\nPatient: Yes… not completely take over, but my daughter has started checking behind me, which is hard to admit. She’ll ask whether a bill was paid, or she’ll look over the appointments with me, because she doesn’t really trust that I’ll keep it all straight on my own anymore. And I can’t say she’s wrong, even though it bothers me.\n\nThere was also a big event at the senior center that I used to lead, and I had to give that up. It involved too many moving pieces — times, people to call, little arrangements — and I just wasn’t managing it reliably. I felt embarrassed, because I’d done things like that before and I liked being useful, but it got to the point where I was afraid I’d miss something important.\n\nSo… yes, I guess I haven’t had someone fully take over my life, but I do need more oversight now than I used to.\n\nDoctor: Have you had trouble finding the right words when you’re speaking?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure, honestly. I mean… everyone has moments where a word is on the tip of their tongue, don’t they? I’ll sometimes pause and say, “Oh, what’s that called again?” but I don’t know that it’s been something I’d point to as a real problem.\n\nI haven’t noticed myself regularly using the wrong words or being unable to get a sentence out. At least, no one has really said to me, “You’re having trouble talking,” or anything like that. It’s more just the ordinary kind of searching for a name or a word now and then, as far as I can tell.\n\nSo… I don’t think so, not in any major way.\n\nDoctor: Do you have more trouble learning new information now than you used to?\n\nPatient: I’m not really sure how to answer that. I don’t think I’ve noticed a clear change where I’d say, “Oh, I can’t learn things anymore,” if that’s what you mean. It’s more that if someone tells me something new, I may need it repeated, or I may want to write it down, but I don’t know if that’s learning exactly or just me not keeping it in my head the first time.\n\nIf it’s something I’m interested in and I can take my time with it, I think I can still pick it up. But if someone explains something quickly, especially with a lot of steps, I can get a little overwhelmed and then I’m not sure I absorbed it properly. I wouldn’t say I’ve sat down and tested myself, though, so it’s hard for me to compare.\n\nSo… maybe a little, but I can’t say for certain that learning new information itself is worse. I just notice I need more time and reminders than I used to.\n\nDoctor: Do you often forget conversations or events that happened just a short time earlier, even after someone has already told you them?\n\nPatient: I don’t know that I’d say I “often” forget whole conversations or events right after they happen. I mean, there are times when someone will say, “I told you that,” and I’ll have this awful feeling because I truly don’t remember the moment they said it, or I only remember it once they give me a lot of hints. But I’m not sure how often is often, if that makes sense.\n\nSometimes I think maybe I wasn’t fully paying attention when they told me, so then later it looks like I forgot, but maybe I never really took it in properly in the first place. Like if someone tells me something while I’m doing something else, or if there are a lot of little details, then yes, I may need them to tell me again. But if it’s a big event or a real conversation where I’m sitting there focused, I usually have some sense of it afterward.\n\nSo… I guess I do have moments like that, and they bother me, but I’m not sure I can say I’m forgetting entire recent conversations all the time. It’s more uneven than that.\n\nDoctor: Do you find that you forget things you were just told even when you were paying close attention at the time?\n\nPatient: I’m not completely sure. But then later, sometimes it’s fuzzier than I expected, and I’ll think, “Wait, did they say Tuesday or Thursday?” or “Was I supposed to call them, or were they calling me?” So I don’t know if that counts as forgetting what I was just told, or if it’s more that the details don’t stick very well.\n\nIt’s hard because I can feel like I’m listening. I’m nodding, I’m following along, I may even repeat it back in my head. But then afterward, unless I wrote it down or there’s something to remind me, some part of it may just sort of… slip away. But yes, there are times when I’m surprised by how little stayed with me, even though I thought I was paying attention.\n\nDoctor: Have family members or friends told you that your thinking or memory has clearly changed from how you used to be?\n\nPatient: I don’t think anyone has said it in that clear a way, like, “Your thinking has changed,” or “Your memory is worse than it used to be.” Not that I can remember, anyway. People close to me may get frustrated if I ask something again or if I don’t keep track of what was said, but I don’t know that they’ve described it as a definite change.\n\nThat’s part of what makes it hard for me to answer, because I’m not always the best judge of what other people are noticing.
